report:
Based on the evidence, here's my assessment of that health claim.

## What the evidence shows

**Observational studies suggest a modest protective association.** A large meta-analysis in *Heart* pooling prospective cohort studies found chocolate consumption was inversely associated with cardiovascular disease risk, including stroke, though the relationship appeared non-linear with diminishing benefit at higher intakes (https://heart.bmj.com/content/105/1/49). A dedicated meta-analysis of chocolate and coronary heart disease/stroke similarly reported reduced risk with higher chocolate intake (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/9/7/688). Individual cohort and case-control studies (e.g., in *Neurology* and *Atherosclerosis*) report similar inverse associations, particularly for higher-quality (dark) chocolate.

**Mechanistic plausibility exists.** Cocoa flavanols improve endothelial function, nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, blood pressure, and cerebral/peripheral blood flow — all biologically relevant to stroke risk (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11992872/).

**However, causal proof is weak.** The large-scale randomized COSMOS trial testing cocoa flavanol supplements found a reduction in cardiovascular *death* but did not show a significant reduction in stroke or overall major cardiovascular events. A Mendelian randomization study on dark chocolate and cardiovascular disease also produced mixed/limited causal evidence (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10781976/).

## Bottom line

The claim is **plausible but not firmly established**. Observational data and biological mechanisms support a modest inverse association between chocolate (especially dark, flavanol-rich) intake and stroke risk, but confounding (chocolate eaters may have healthier overall diets/lifestyles) is a concern, and the best available randomized trial evidence hasn't confirmed a clear stroke-specific benefit. Moderate dark chocolate consumption is unlikely to be harmful and may offer some cardiovascular benefit, but it shouldn't be considered a proven stroke-prevention strategy.
